answers.question: Given a single non-negative integer N, draw a flowchart to calculate and print N factorial (N!), the product of all integers from 1 to N inclusive. Start, read N, initialize result = 1 and i = 1, loop while i <= N doing result = result * i and i = i + 1, print result, End. Special case: 0! = 1, so the loop simply does not execute. Input: 5, Expected Output: 120.
answers.shortTitle: Factorial — print N! as the product of all integers from 1 to N

s1_definition.profdef: The factorial of a non-negative integer N, written N!, is the product of every integer from 1 up to N. By definition 0! equals 1 because the product of no numbers at all is the multiplicative identity, which is one. The standard iterative algorithm keeps a running product starting at one and multiplies it by each integer from one to N, which naturally handles the zero case because the loop body never runs.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India calculating how many different orders N pending cheques can be processed in. The first cheque can go in any of N slots, the next in any of the remaining N minus one slots, and so on down to one. Multiplying those shrinking choices together is exactly a factorial. Rajesh asks how many ways his five cheques can be arranged, and the answer is five times four times three times two times one, which is 120.
s1_definition.oneliner: Factorial is a running product that starts at one and multiplies in every integer from one to N, and because an empty product is one, zero factorial is one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The factorial of a non-negative integer N, written N!, is the product of every integer from 1 up to N. By definition 0! equals 1 because the product of no numbers at all is the multiplicative identity, which is one. The standard iterative algorithm keeps a running product starting at one and multiplies it by each integer from one to N, which naturally handles the zero case because the loop body never runs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India calculating how many different orders N pending cheques can be processed in. The first cheque can go in any of N slots, the next in any of the remaining N minus one slots, and so on down to one. Multiplying those shrinking choices together is exactly a factorial. Rajesh asks how many ways his five cheques can be arranged, and the answer is five times four times three times two times one, which is 120.

**One line to remember:** Factorial is a running product that starts at one and multiplies in every integer from one to N, and because an empty product is one, zero factorial is one.

sections.s2_technical:
The algorithm needs one accumulator and one counter. You start the accumulator, call it result, at one, because one is the neutral value for multiplication. You then walk a counter i from one to N inclusive, and on each step you do result = result * i. When the loop finishes, result holds N!.

A critical detail for a banking system is overflow. Factorials grow extremely fast, and a Java long overflows past 20!. Because money and counts in banking must never silently wrap into a negative or wrong number, I compute factorials with BigInteger, which has arbitrary precision and never overflows. For example, `BigInteger result = BigInteger.ONE; result = result.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(i));` keeps multiplying safely no matter how large the value gets.

The zero case falls out for free. If N is zero, the loop condition i <= N is one <= zero, which is false immediately, so the body never runs and result stays at its initial value of one. That is exactly the mathematical definition of 0!, so no special branch is needed in the code, though I still validate that N is not negative because factorial is undefined for negative numbers and I reject that with a clear exception.

The time complexity is linear in N because we do one multiplication per step, and the space is constant apart from the size of the big number itself. A senior nuance is that for repeated queries you can cache previously computed factorials, and for very large N you would switch to specialized libraries, but for the arrangement counts a bank actually needs, the simple linear loop with BigInteger is correct and clear.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The operations desk at National Bank of India wants to know, for audit sampling, how many distinct orders a small batch of N cheques could be processed in. The number of orderings of N items is exactly N factorial, so we need a correct factorial routine.

This is exactly how the factorial algorithm works, because arranging N distinct things in a line gives N choices for the first, N minus one for the second, and so on, and that product is N!.

Problem 2 — Factorials explode in size and a plain long silently overflows past twenty, which in a bank would produce a wrong or negative count and a false audit figure. This is exactly why we compute with BigInteger, which never overflows.

Problem 3 — A batch might be empty, meaning zero cheques, and the system must report exactly one ordering, not crash. This is exactly the 0! equals 1 case that the loop handles naturally by never executing.

Our mini-project builds a `FactorialCalculator` service with a `factorial(int n)` method returning BigInteger, validation rejecting negative input, and a `FactorialDemo` runnable that computes the arrangements for Rajesh's batch of five cheques and prints 120.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: N = 5 (Rajesh's batch of five cheques).

Step 1 — The accumulator result is initialized to one and the counter i to one. At this point no multiplication has happened, so result represents the empty product.

Step 2 — The loop checks i <= N, which is 1 <= 5, true. It multiplies result by i, giving 1 times 1 equals 1, then increments i to two.

Step 3 — Next iterations multiply in 2, 3, 4, and 5 in turn. result becomes 2, then 6, then 24, then 120, while i climbs to 6.

Step 4 — The loop checks 6 <= 5, which is false, so the loop stops. The accumulator result holds 120, which is 5!.

Step 5 — For the empty batch, N is zero, so the very first check 1 <= 0 is false, the body never runs, and result stays at one, correctly giving 0! equals 1.

Step 6 — The service returns BigInteger values, so even a large batch would be computed exactly without overflow, and the demo logs both results.

Final output:

```
2026-10-31 23:40:00 [INFO] Rajesh SAV2001: 5 cheques can be processed in 120 distinct orders
2026-10-31 23:40:00 [INFO] Empty batch 0! = 1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Factorial of a non-negative integer N is the product of every integer from one up to N, and by definition zero factorial is one because the product of no numbers is the multiplicative identity. The iterative algorithm is simple and reliable: you start a running product at one, then multiply it by each integer from one to N, and when the loop finishes the running product is the answer. The zero case needs no special code, because when N is zero the loop condition fails immediately, the body never runs, and the product stays at its initial value of one, which is exactly the mathematical definition.

The real-world subtlety that matters in a bank is overflow. Factorials grow astonishingly fast, and a Java long overflows past twenty factorial, which would silently produce a wrong or even negative number. In a financial system a silently wrong count is unacceptable, so I compute factorials with BigInteger, which has arbitrary precision and never overflows. I also add a guard clause that rejects negative input with a clear exception, because factorial is simply undefined there.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, I used this for an audit-sampling tool where the operations desk needed to know how many distinct orders a small batch of cheques could be processed in, which is exactly the number of arrangements of N items, so N factorial. I wrote a FactorialCalculator with a single factorial method returning a BigInteger, validated the input, and let the loop handle the empty-batch case naturally. When Rajesh submitted five cheques the tool reported one hundred and twenty orderings, and because I used BigInteger it would stay exact even for much larger batches. The lesson I carry from this is that even the simplest arithmetic needs the right numeric type, and in finance that almost always means an overflow-safe type rather than a primitive.

answers.question: Draw a flowchart that reads two numbers A and B, computes their sum, and prints the result. Start, read A, read B, sum = A + B, print sum, End. Input: 4 7, Expected Output: 11.
answers.shortTitle: Add Two Numbers — read A and B, print their sum

s1_definition.profdef: Adding two numbers is the most basic arithmetic operation: read two operands, apply the addition operator to produce their sum, and output it. In a financial context the operands are monetary amounts, so the correct type is BigDecimal with an explicit scale and rounding policy rather than a floating-point primitive, because binary floating point cannot represent decimal fractions like paise exactly.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh deposits 4 thousand rupees in the morning and 7 thousand rupees in the afternoon, and National Bank of India needs the day's total credited to his savings account SAV2001. The teller simply adds the two amounts, four plus seven, and records eleven thousand. That single addition, done with exact decimal arithmetic, is the whole operation.
s1_definition.oneliner: Adding two numbers is read, add, print, but in banking the amounts must be BigDecimal so the sum of money is exact to the paisa.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Adding two numbers is the most basic arithmetic operation: read two operands, apply the addition operator to produce their sum, and output it. In a financial context the operands are monetary amounts, so the correct type is BigDecimal with an explicit scale and rounding policy rather than a floating-point primitive, because binary floating point cannot represent decimal fractions like paise exactly.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh deposits 4 thousand rupees in the morning and 7 thousand rupees in the afternoon, and National Bank of India needs the day's total credited to his savings account SAV2001. The teller simply adds the two amounts, four plus seven, and records eleven thousand. That single addition, done with exact decimal arithmetic, is the whole operation.

**One line to remember:** Adding two numbers is read, add, print, but in banking the amounts must be BigDecimal so the sum of money is exact to the paisa.

sections.s2_technical:
The algorithm reads two values into A and B, computes sum = A + B, and prints sum. For integers you would just use the plus operator, but for money you must not. Floating-point types like double store values in binary, and common decimal amounts such as 0.10 cannot be represented exactly, so repeated addition drifts and a bank statement ends up a paisa wrong. That is why every monetary amount in my code is a BigDecimal.

With BigDecimal you add using the `add` method rather than the plus operator, for example `BigDecimal sum = a.add(b);`. BigDecimal keeps an unscaled value and a scale, so if A is 4000.00 and B is 7000.00 the result is 11000.00 with the scale preserved. When displaying or persisting money I set a fixed scale of two with a defined rounding mode, for example `sum.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)`, so the stored amount always has exactly two decimal places.

Input handling matters too. In a real service the two numbers arrive as request fields or as strings parsed from a message, and I construct BigDecimal from the String form, not from a double, because `new BigDecimal(0.1)` captures the binary error whereas `new BigDecimal("0.1")` is exact. A senior nuance is validation: amounts should be non-negative for a deposit total, parsing failures must be rejected with a clear error, and the addition itself cannot overflow because BigDecimal has arbitrary precision, which is one more reason it is the right choice for money.

Problem 2 — The amounts are money, and if we add them as doubles the total can drift by a fraction of a paisa, which is unacceptable on a statement. This is exactly why the addition uses BigDecimal with the add method and a fixed two-decimal scale.

Problem 3 — The amounts arrive as text from the deposit slips, and parsing must be exact and must reject garbage. This is exactly why we build BigDecimal from the String form and validate it.

Our mini-project builds a `DepositTotalService` with an `addAmounts(BigDecimal a, BigDecimal b)` method and a `DepositDemo` runnable that totals Rajesh's two deposits of 4000 and 7000 and prints 11000.00.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Adding two numbers is the simplest operation there is: read the first operand, read the second, apply the addition operator, and print the sum. The flowchart is literally read A, read B, compute sum equals A plus B, and print. But the moment those two numbers are money, the naive approach becomes a bug, and that is the point I always make.

Floating-point types like double store numbers in binary, and ordinary decimal amounts such as ten paise cannot be represented exactly, so adding money as doubles slowly drifts and a statement ends up a fraction wrong. In banking that is never acceptable, so every monetary amount in my code is a BigDecimal, I add with the add method rather than the plus operator, and I build BigDecimal from the String form rather than from a double so the value is captured exactly. I also fix the result to two decimal places with an explicit rounding mode so the stored total always has exactly a rupees-and-paise shape, and I validate that the inputs are present and non-negative before adding.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this was the deposit-total feature where Rajesh made two deposits into his savings account on the same day and we needed the combined figure credited exactly. I wrote a DepositTotalService whose addAmounts method takes two BigDecimal values, validates them, adds them, and sets the scale to two with half-even rounding. His four thousand and seven thousand rupees totaled exactly eleven thousand rupees with two decimal places, and because the whole path used BigDecimal there was no possibility of a rounding drift. The lesson is that even addition is a place where choosing BigDecimal over a primitive is the difference between a correct ledger and a slowly corrupting one.

answers.question: Given three numbers, draw a flowchart to calculate and print their average value. Start, read A, read B, read C, sum = A + B + C, average = sum / 3, print average, End. Input: 10 20 30, Expected Output: 20.
answers.shortTitle: Average — read three numbers and print their average

s1_definition.profdef: The average, or arithmetic mean, of a set of values is their sum divided by their count. For three values the algorithm adds A, B, and C, then divides the total by three. With money this division is the dangerous step, because it can produce a non-terminating decimal, so it must be done with BigDecimal using an explicit scale and rounding mode rather than a floating-point division that would silently lose precision.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants the average monthly balance Rajesh kept in SAV2001 over three months to decide his interest tier. The bank adds the three monthly balances and divides by three. If the three balances are ten, twenty, and thirty thousand, the average is twenty thousand. The only care needed is that division of money must round to a fixed number of paise in a defined way.
s1_definition.oneliner: Average is sum divided by count, and for money the division must use BigDecimal with an explicit scale and rounding mode so the result is well defined.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The average, or arithmetic mean, of a set of values is their sum divided by their count. For three values the algorithm adds A, B, and C, then divides the total by three. With money this division is the dangerous step, because it can produce a non-terminating decimal, so it must be done with BigDecimal using an explicit scale and rounding mode rather than a floating-point division that would silently lose precision.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India wants the average monthly balance Rajesh kept in SAV2001 over three months to decide his interest tier. The bank adds the three monthly balances and divides by three. If the three balances are ten, twenty, and thirty thousand, the average is twenty thousand. The only care needed is that division of money must round to a fixed number of paise in a defined way.

**One line to remember:** Average is sum divided by count, and for money the division must use BigDecimal with an explicit scale and rounding mode so the result is well defined.

sections.s2_technical:
The algorithm reads the three values, computes their sum, then divides by three. The addition is straightforward with BigDecimal's add method. The division is where correctness is decided. BigDecimal's `divide` method with only the divisor throws an ArithmeticException if the result is a non-terminating decimal, for example dividing ten by three. That is actually a helpful safety feature, because it forces you to decide how to round. So I always call the overload that takes a scale and a RoundingMode, for example `sum.divide(new BigDecimal("3"), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)`, which yields a result fixed to two decimals.

The divisor is the count of values, three here, and it is exact. The sum is exact because it is a BigDecimal addition. Only the division can introduce rounding, and by specifying scale two and half-even rounding I get a banker's-rounding result that does not bias repeatedly up or down over many calculations, which is the convention real banks use for money.

Validation and ordering do not matter for an average because addition is commutative, but input validity does. I reject null amounts and, depending on the business rule, negative balances. A senior nuance is that for a true weighted average, such as a time-weighted average balance where each balance is held for a different number of days, you multiply each balance by its weight before summing and divide by the total weight, but for this equal-weight three-value case the plain sum over three is exactly right.

Problem 1 — National Bank of India needs the average of Rajesh's three monthly closing balances to assign an interest tier. We must add the three balances and divide by three. This is exactly the sum = A + B + C, average = sum / 3 algorithm.

Problem 2 — Dividing money by three can produce a repeating decimal, and a naive BigDecimal divide would throw or a double divide would silently round wrong. This is exactly why the division specifies a scale of two and half-even rounding.

Problem 3 — The tier decision must be reproducible and unbiased across thousands of accounts. This is exactly why half-even banker's rounding is used so repeated averages do not drift upward.

Our mini-project builds an `AverageBalanceService` with an `average(BigDecimal a, BigDecimal b, BigDecimal c)` method and an `AverageDemo` runnable that averages 10000, 20000, and 30000 and prints 20000.00.

The addition is trivial, but for money the division is the step that decides correctness, and that is where I focus.

With BigDecimal, calling divide with only the divisor throws an ArithmeticException whenever the result is a non-terminating decimal, such as dividing ten by three, which is actually a useful safety net because it forces an explicit decision. answers.question: Given a number N, draw a flowchart to check and print whether it is even or odd. Start, read N, decision N % 2 == 0, Yes print Even, No print Odd, End. Input: 7, Expected Output: Odd.
answers.shortTitle: Even or Odd — check and print whether N is even or odd

s1_definition.profdef: A number is even when it is exactly divisible by two, meaning the remainder of dividing it by two is zero, and odd otherwise. The test is the modulo operation N % 2, where a result of zero means even and a result of one means odd. For a correct implementation on signed integers you check the remainder against zero rather than against one, because negative odd numbers give a remainder of minus one in Java.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India routes transactions to one of two processing queues to balance load, sending even-numbered transaction IDs to queue A and odd ones to queue B. To decide where Rajesh's transaction with ID seven goes, the system checks whether seven divided by two leaves a remainder. Seven leaves remainder one, so it is odd and goes to queue B.
s1_definition.oneliner: A number is even when its remainder on division by two is zero and odd otherwise, and you should test the remainder against zero so negative numbers are handled correctly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A number is even when it is exactly divisible by two, meaning the remainder of dividing it by two is zero, and odd otherwise. The test is the modulo operation N % 2, where a result of zero means even and a result of one means odd. For a correct implementation on signed integers you check the remainder against zero rather than against one, because negative odd numbers give a remainder of minus one in Java.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India routes transactions to one of two processing queues to balance load, sending even-numbered transaction IDs to queue A and odd ones to queue B. To decide where Rajesh's transaction with ID seven goes, the system checks whether seven divided by two leaves a remainder. Seven leaves remainder one, so it is odd and goes to queue B.

**One line to remember:** A number is even when its remainder on division by two is zero and odd otherwise, and you should test the remainder against zero so negative numbers are handled correctly.

sections.s2_technical:
The core operation is the modulo operator, written with the percent sign. The expression N % 2 gives the remainder when N is divided by two. If that remainder equals zero the number is even, otherwise it is odd. The decision in the flowchart is simply N % 2 == 0, taking the Yes branch to print Even and the No branch to print Odd.

A subtle correctness point in Java is the sign of the modulo result. In Java the remainder takes the sign of the dividend, so minus seven modulo two is minus one, not one. If you wrote a test like N % 2 == 1 to detect odd numbers, it would wrongly classify negative odd numbers as even. The robust test is N % 2 == 0 for even and everything else is odd, which works for positive, negative, and zero. Zero itself is even because zero modulo two is zero.

For a banking identifier like a transaction sequence number this is used for simple partitioning or alternating assignment. For the input seven, seven modulo two is one, which is not zero, so the output is Odd.

The subtle point I always raise is the sign of the remainder in Java. Java's remainder takes the sign of the dividend, so minus seven modulo two is minus one rather than one. If you naively tested for odd by comparing the remainder to one, you would misclassify every negative odd number. For example `a.compareTo(b) > 0` is true when A is strictly greater.

Validation includes rejecting null amounts. A senior nuance is that Java also offers `a.max(b)` on BigDecimal, which returns the larger of the two directly and is the cleanest way to express this in production code, internally doing the compareTo for you. s1_definition.profdef: The largest of three values is found with nested comparisons: if A is at least as large as both B and C, A is the maximum, otherwise the larger of B and C is the maximum, decided by comparing B against C. Using greater-than-or-equal rather than strict greater-than ensures ties are handled without falling through. For money the comparisons use BigDecimal's compareTo so numeric value, not scale, decides the winner.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India reviews three competing interest-rate offers for Rajesh's fixed deposit and must present the best one. The three offers are five, eighteen, and eleven percent equivalents. The system compares them and picks eighteen, the highest, as the offer to apply.
s1_definition.oneliner: The largest of three comes from nested comparisons using greater-than-or-equal, first testing whether A beats both others, else choosing the larger of B and C.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The largest of three values is found with nested comparisons: if A is at least as large as both B and C, A is the maximum, otherwise the larger of B and C is the maximum, decided by comparing B against C. Using greater-than-or-equal rather than strict greater-than ensures ties are handled without falling through. For money the comparisons use BigDecimal's compareTo so numeric value, not scale, decides the winner.

sections.s2_technical:
The algorithm reads A, B, and C and uses a two-level decision. The first decision asks whether A is at least as large as B and at least as large as C, written A greater-than-or-equal B and A greater-than-or-equal C. If both hold, A is the maximum. If not, the second decision compares B and C: if B is at least as large as C, B is the maximum, otherwise C is. Using greater-than-or-equal rather than strict greater-than is important because it guarantees that when two or three values tie, one of them is still selected rather than the logic slipping through with no answer.

For money the three amounts are BigDecimal and every comparison uses compareTo. The combined first condition becomes `a.compareTo(b) >= 0 && a.compareTo(c) >= 0`, and the inner one becomes `b.compareTo(c) >= 0`. Using compareTo rather than equals or the relational operators is essential because relational operators do not work on objects and equals would be scale-sensitive. compareTo compares pure numeric value.

A cleaner production alternative is to use BigDecimal's max method twice, `a.max(b).max(c)`, which chains to give the maximum of all three without any branches, and that is what I would ship, but the nested-decision form shown here mirrors the flowchart and makes the reasoning explicit. A senior nuance is to validate all three inputs are present, and to be clear about tie behavior with the business, since greater-than-or-equal means that on a tie the earliest listed value wins, which is a deliberate and documented choice.

The flowchart uses two nested decisions: first test whether N is greater than zero and return one, otherwise test whether N is less than zero and return minus one, and the final else can only be the exact-zero case, so it returns zero. An important related point is that the net movement itself should be computed in BigDecimal throughout, because a floating-point sum of many debits and credits can land on a tiny nonzero value and wrongly flip a flat day into a movement, whereas an exact BigDecimal sum gives a clean zero and a correct flat label.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, I used this for a dashboard that shows whether an account moved up, down, or stayed flat for the day. I wrote a MovementClassifier whose sign method takes the net BigDecimal movement and returns plus one, minus one, or zero using signum. For Rajesh, a net debit of eight thousand classified as minus one and the dashboard drew a down arrow, and a genuinely no-change day would classify as zero and draw a flat line. sections.s2_technical:
The rule has three parts combined into one boolean expression. Divisible by four is the base rule. The exception removes century years, those divisible by one hundred, because most of them are not leap years. The exception to the exception restores century years that are divisible by four hundred, which are leap years. Written out, the condition is (year modulo four equals zero and year modulo one hundred is not zero) or (year modulo four hundred equals zero). If the whole expression is true the year is a leap year.

You can check this manually with modulo, and that is what the flowchart shows, but in production Java I would use `java.time.Year.of(year).isLeap()`, which implements the exact Gregorian rule and removes any chance of getting the operator precedence or the exceptions wrong. For example `Year.of(2000).isLeap()` returns true and `Year.of(1900).isLeap()` returns false. Relying on the standard library here is the senior choice because date rules are notoriously easy to get subtly wrong.

In banking this feeds day-count conventions for interest. An actual-over-actual convention uses the real number of days in the year, so leap-year detection changes the denominator from three hundred sixty-five to three hundred sixty-six, which changes the interest figure. A senior nuance is that different products use different conventions, such as thirty over three hundred sixty, and the leap-year rule only matters for the actual-days conventions, so I keep the day-count logic explicit and well tested, and I validate the year is sensible before using it.

A triangle is valid if and only if the sum of any two sides is greater than the third (A + B > C and B + C > A and C + A > B). answers.shortTitle: Form Triangle — print Yes if three lengths can form a valid triangle

s1_definition.profdef: Three positive lengths can form a triangle if and only if they satisfy the triangle inequality, which requires that the sum of every pair of sides be strictly greater than the remaining side. The algorithm checks all three inequalities joined by logical and, and prints Yes only if all three hold. Strict greater-than is required because equality produces a degenerate, flat triangle.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India runs a validation rule where three separate limits, a daily limit, a weekly sub-limit, and a transaction cap, must be mutually consistent so no single limit dominates the other two combined, mirroring the triangle inequality. For values three, four, and five the limits are balanced and the rule passes with Yes, but one, two, and ten is lopsided and fails with No.
s1_definition.oneliner: Three lengths form a triangle only when every pair sums to strictly more than the third side, checked as three and-joined inequalities.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Three positive lengths can form a triangle if and only if they satisfy the triangle inequality, which requires that the sum of every pair of sides be strictly greater than the remaining side. The algorithm checks all three inequalities joined by logical and, and prints Yes only if all three hold. Strict greater-than is required because equality produces a degenerate, flat triangle.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India runs a validation rule where three separate limits, a daily limit, a weekly sub-limit, and a transaction cap, must be mutually consistent so no single limit dominates the other two combined, mirroring the triangle inequality. For values three, four, and five the limits are balanced and the rule passes with Yes, but one, two, and ten is lopsided and fails with No.

**One line to remember:** Three lengths form a triangle only when every pair sums to strictly more than the third side, checked as three and-joined inequalities.

sections.s2_technical:
The triangle inequality has three conditions: A plus B greater than C, B plus C greater than A, and C plus A greater than B. All three must hold simultaneously, so they are combined with logical and. If any one fails, the three lengths cannot close into a triangle. The strictness matters: if a pair sums to exactly the third side, the three points are collinear and the triangle is degenerate with zero area, so we require strictly greater-than and reject equality.

With money-like BigDecimal values, each addition uses the add method and each comparison uses compareTo. The condition `a.add(b).compareTo(c) > 0` expresses A plus B greater than C. I compute all three and combine with and. I also validate that all three lengths are positive, because a zero or negative length is not a valid side at all; some implementations fold that into the inequality, but an explicit positivity check gives a clearer error.

A performance and clarity nuance is that if the sides are sorted so that C is the largest, then only the single check A plus B greater than C needs to be verified, because the other two inequalities are automatically satisfied when C is the maximum. That optimization is common in interviews, but for three values the cost is negligible and checking all three explicitly is clearer, so I keep all three unless profiling says otherwise. Throughout, using BigDecimal with compareTo avoids any floating-point comparison error near the boundary.

Problem 2 — A boundary case where one value equals the sum of the other two must be rejected as invalid, just like a degenerate triangle. This is exactly why the comparisons are strictly greater-than.

Problem 3 — The limits are decimal amounts, so comparisons must be numeric and exact. This is exactly why each check uses BigDecimal add and compareTo.

Our mini-project builds a `TriangleValidator` with a `canFormTriangle(BigDecimal a, BigDecimal b, BigDecimal c)` method and a `FormTriangleDemo` runnable that validates three, four, five as Yes and one, two, ten as No.

Three lengths can form a triangle if and only if they satisfy the triangle inequality, which requires that the sum of every pair of sides be strictly greater than the remaining side. So the condition is A plus B greater than C, and B plus C greater than A, and C plus A greater than B, all three combined with logical and. The flowchart reads the three lengths, evaluates that compound condition, and prints Yes when all three hold or No otherwise. For three, four, and five all three inequalities hold, so the answer is Yes, while one, two, and ten fails the first inequality and gives No.

The detail I always stress is strictness. The comparisons must be strictly greater-than, because if a pair sums to exactly the third side the three points are collinear and the triangle is degenerate with no area, which is not a valid triangle. I also validate that all three lengths are positive, since a zero or negative side is meaningless. A known optimization is that if you sort so the largest side is last, you only need to check one inequality, but for three values I keep all three for clarity.

A balanced set like three, four, five passed, while a lopsided set like one, two, ten was rejected. The lesson is that the triangle inequality is really a general balance condition, and implementing it with strict comparisons and exact arithmetic makes it a dependable validation building block.

Start, read N, initialize product = 1 and i = 1, loop while i <= N doing product = product * i and i = i + 1, print product, End. Special case: 0! = 1, the loop does not execute. Input: 4, Expected Output: 24.
answers.shortTitle: Understanding Loop (Product) — compute N! using a loop

s1_definition.profdef: This problem demonstrates a multiplicative accumulation loop: a running product is initialized to one, the loop multiplies it by each integer from one to N, and the final product is N factorial. It teaches the fundamental loop pattern of an accumulator plus a counter, where the accumulator's starting value is the identity element of the operation, which for multiplication is one.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India computes a compounding growth factor by multiplying a sequence of per-period multipliers together, which is the same loop shape as a factorial, a running product updated each step. To understand the pattern, we compute four factorial by multiplying one by two by three by four, which gives twenty-four.
s1_definition.oneliner: A product loop starts the accumulator at one, the multiplicative identity, and multiplies in each value, which is why an empty product and zero factorial are both one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem demonstrates a multiplicative accumulation loop: a running product is initialized to one, the loop multiplies it by each integer from one to N, and the final product is N factorial. It teaches the fundamental loop pattern of an accumulator plus a counter, where the accumulator's starting value is the identity element of the operation, which for multiplication is one.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India computes a compounding growth factor by multiplying a sequence of per-period multipliers together, which is the same loop shape as a factorial, a running product updated each step. To understand the pattern, we compute four factorial by multiplying one by two by three by four, which gives twenty-four.

**One line to remember:** A product loop starts the accumulator at one, the multiplicative identity, and multiplies in each value, which is why an empty product and zero factorial are both one.

sections.s2_technical:
The loop pattern has two variables: an accumulator named product and a counter named i. The accumulator starts at one because one is the identity for multiplication, meaning multiplying by it changes nothing, which makes it the correct seed. The counter starts at one and the loop continues while i is less than or equal to N. Each iteration performs product = product * i and then increments i. When the loop ends, product holds the product of all integers from one to N, which is N factorial.

The key teaching point versus an addition loop is the choice of identity: for a sum you start the accumulator at zero, but for a product you start at one, because starting a product at zero would make everything zero. Getting the identity wrong is a classic beginner bug, and this problem exists to make that lesson concrete. The zero case also falls out naturally: when N is zero the condition one less-than-or-equal zero is false, the body never runs, and product stays at one, correctly giving zero factorial equals one.

For banking I compute the running product with BigInteger for exact integer factorials, or BigDecimal when multiplying decimal growth factors, because both avoid overflow and precision loss that plain primitives would suffer. A senior nuance is that this accumulate-in-a-loop pattern generalizes directly to compounding interest, where you multiply balance by one plus the rate each period, so understanding the product loop is the foundation for a whole family of financial calculations, and I always keep the accumulator's type wide enough to hold the growing result.

Problem 3 — An empty input, N equals zero, must return one, not crash. This is exactly the loop-does-not-execute case that leaves product at its seed of one.

This problem is really about understanding the product-loop pattern, which is an accumulator and a counter working together. You seed the accumulator, call it product, to one, then run a counter from one to N, and on each step you multiply the accumulator by the counter, so when the loop ends the accumulator holds the product of all integers from one to N, which is N factorial. sections.s2_technical:
The basic algorithm sets a boolean isPrime to true and tries candidate divisors i starting at two. For each i it checks whether N modulo i equals zero; if so, i divides N evenly, N is composite, so isPrime becomes false and the loop can break immediately because one factor is enough to decide. If the loop finishes without finding a divisor, N is prime.

The crucial optimization is the loop bound. Testing i while i is less than N works but is wasteful. It is enough to test while i times i is less than or equal to N, that is up to the square root of N, because divisors come in pairs that multiply to N, and one member of each pair is always at or below the square root. So if no divisor is found up to the square root, none exists above it either. This changes the cost from linear in N to the square root of N, which is a huge saving for large values, and I always write the condition as `i * i <= n` to avoid computing a floating-point square root.

Edge handling matters: numbers below two are not prime by definition, two is the only even prime, and after checking two you could step i by two to skip even candidates for a further speedup. For the very large primes used in cryptographic key sizes, trial division is far too slow and you use probabilistic tests like Miller-Rabin, which is what BigInteger's isProbablePrime method does, and that is the senior-level choice for real key material. For small configuration parameters, the square-root trial-division loop shown here is correct and clear.
